18.0.0.en: David organized his army and appointed commanders over its divisions; although his army was small in number, he organized it with military skill.

18.1.0.en: David divided his forces into three divisions headed by Joab, Abishai and Ittai the Gittite, and David wanted to go out himself to the field of battle to lead them all as supreme commander.

18.2.0.en: The people insisted that David not go out to the field of battle, because he would be the target sought by Absalom and his men. They told him that if half of their men fled from the field or were killed, the enemy would not care about them, but in his being wounded or killed would be the end, and victory would be achieved for Absalom, since his life meant the continuance of his kingdom.

18.3.0.en: David acted according to his people's counsel, so he stood beside the gate of the city, and the men of his army went out in ranks and orderly numbers, according to the division David himself had made before, so that each company consisted of a hundred fighters headed by a commander, and every ten companies made a thousand fighters headed by a greater commander, and each third was headed by one of the three commanders he had appointed before (v. 2).

18.4.0.en: Despite all that Absalom had done against his father of rebellion and disobedience, the merciful father's heart feared that harm might touch his son, so he charged his commanders that if Absalom fell into their hands they were not to insult him or kill him, and the men of his army heard him as he commanded the commanders concerning his son.

18.4.1.en: Is this not an example of what the Lord of glory did with us sinners, for while we were yet sinners He gave His only Son as a redemption for us, and forgave even those who crucified Him while He was on the Cross? So be merciful and make excuses for those who wrong you; for just as the devil made them fall into evil, he can make you fall; and ask for God's help and mercy for yourself and for them, and you will be like your Lord Christ.

18.5.0.en: Wood: the wood is land thick with trees, in addition to pits, difficult roads and wild beasts.

18.5.1.en: The wood of Ephraim: Ephraim dwells west of the Jordan and this place is east of the Jordan, and it was so called because Ephraim was defeated in it before Jephthah and the Gileadites (Judg 12:6); and this place is not the wood of Ephraim that is west of the Jordan (Josh 17:18). David's men went out to meet Absalom's army, and the field of battle was the thickly wooded lands of Ephraim.

18.6.0.en: Absalom's men were severely defeated there, and a slaughter took place in which twenty thousand were slain, most of them from Absalom's army. This victory was due to God's help to David and his wronged men, and the Lord used the skill of David's men in war, while Absalom's men were less trained than they.

18.7.0.en: The field of battle was broad, spread over a large area of land, and the flight of the men of Absalom's army was disorderly, so they scattered in the surrounding forests, and most of them died of hunger and thirst and unfavorable weather conditions, so that they were more than those who were slain by the swords of David's men. God saved David's men from the wood because they were defending their good king, and He allowed the death of many in Israel's army because they were enemies of David the good king whom God had chosen.

18.8.0.en: The oak: a huge tree with tangled branches.

18.8.1.en: It happened that a fighting party from David's army met Absalom as he was riding on his mule, and as soon as he saw them he was confused and tried to flee quickly from before them, so he went under a great tree with tangled branches, and his long hair became entangled and caught in the branches while the mule went on its way, leaving him in this position. Thus Absalom was left hanging by his hair in the branches of the tree between heaven and earth.

18.9.0.en: One of David's men made sure of Absalom's identity, and hurried to tell Joab his supreme commander that he had seen Absalom hanging in the tree.

18.9.1.en: The hair that was a source of pride and boasting to Absalom was also the cause of the calamity that befell him. Let our adornment not be "the outward adornment but the adornment of the spirit" (1 Pet 3:3).

18.10.0.en: Joab asked him in disapproval why he had not struck him down at once and killed him; if he had done this, he would have given him a valuable reward (150 grams of silver, which was a large sum at that time), in addition to a belt such as is given to one who has shown courage in battle.

18.11.0.en: The man showed his obedience to his king David, and his answer to Joab was that even if the reward to be given him were a hundred times what was mentioned, he would not be willing to do harm to Absalom, and he reminded Joab of the king's strict charge to his commanders not to harm Absalom.

18.12.0.en: I should have wrought falsehood against mine own life: I should have put my life in danger.

18.12.1.en: There is no matter hid from the king: this shows David's strength and wisdom and God's support for him.

18.12.2.en: The man told Joab that if he dared to kill Absalom, he would expose himself to severe punishment by King David, because the king would surely come to know of the matter, and Joab himself would then testify against him that he was the killer.

18.13.0.en: Joab said to the soldier, "I will not waste time speaking with you"; then he took three darts and thrust them into the heart of Absalom, who was still alive and hanging in the tree, and Joab commanded ten of his soldiers to finish killing Absalom; then the ten of Joab's men surrounded him and struck him until he died. In this way responsibility for the killing of Absalom was diffused, since eleven persons took part in killing him, among them the commander of the army, and it would be hard for David to order all of these put to death. Joab did this to protect himself from David's anger when he heard of his son's death. Joab did not obey David's charge because he saw that Absalom's life represented a danger to David's life: if he remained alive despite his defeat, he could try to gather another army as he had done at first and attack David again.

18.13.1.en: Absalom's death was a punishment from God for violating the commandment to honor one's parents, so we must not take lightly that commandment, which is the first commandment with promise, "that thy days may be long upon the land" (Ex 20:12).

18.14.0.en: As soon as Absalom was killed, Joab blew the trumpet announcing the end of the war, and commanded his men not to continue pursuing Absalom's men.

18.14.1.en: David here is a type of Christ, who triumphed over Satan in the battle of the Cross and bound him, as David triumphed over his enemies and Absalom was killed, who is a type of Satan.

18.15.0.en: The end was very sad, for no official funeral was held for Absalom as a prince, and he was not buried even in the tombs of his forefathers or in Jerusalem, and they did not carry him to his father at Mahanaim, but his body was cast into a deep pit in the very forest that had been the scene of the fighting, and they threw stones upon him until they formed a heap of stones, and this was a punishment from heaven for the son's disobedience.

18.16.0.en: The King's Dale: a valley lying east of Jerusalem.

18.16.1.en: Absalom had made for himself a memorial pillar in the King's Dale because he had no son left alive; he set it up with the aim of preserving his memory after his death, and sadly the pillar became a reminder to people of his rebellion and evil, not of his righteousness and purity of heart. More important than building tombs is that a person dwell in righteousness, so that he may have a place in heaven.

18.16.2.en: Among the most important things we must strive to leave behind on earth after our departure is the good remembrance that the people who lived in our time will keep of us, so let us strive that our memory be, as is that of the righteous, for blessing and not for a curse.

18.17.s.en: (3) The news of the war is brought to David

18.17.0.en: Ahimaaz wanted to run to Mahanaim to bring the king David the good news of the victory achieved by his men and the defeat of his enemies, but Joab tried to stop him, advising him not to go, because what he thought was good news for the king would grieve him greatly because of the death of Absalom his son.

18.18.0.en: Cushi: a man from Cush, that is, Ethiopia, and perhaps he was named after his country.

18.18.1.en: Joab called a Cushite man from among his men and commanded him to go and tell the king the news, and he obeyed and bowed down before Joab and ran to tell David what had been achieved on the field of battle.

18.19.0.en: Ahimaaz was very happy with the victory that had been achieved, and he himself had had a part in achieving this victory, since he had earlier informed David of the counsel of Ahithophel and Hushai the Archite, and he remained convinced that the victory was good news worth bringing to the king, so he urged Joab to let him go too after the Cushite, whatever the result. Joab tried once more to stop him from going because he would receive no reward.

18.20.0.en: The way of the plain: the road of the plain.

18.20.1.en: Ahimaaz remained insistent on going to David to tell him of the victory whatever the result, whether he was rewarded or not, and in the face of his insistence Joab allowed him, and Ahimaaz ran, shortly after the Cushite had run for the same purpose, but he took a different road from the one the Cushite took, which was the road of the plain, so that he arrived at David before the Cushite arrived.

18.21.0.en: The two gates: a double wall around the city, each with a gate.

18.21.1.en: The watchman: a person assigned to watch any movements in the area around the city.

18.21.2.en: The wall of the city was a double wall, and each wall had a gate, and David was sitting in the area between the two gates, and the watchman had gone up to the roof over the gate and taken his place on the wall of the city to watch the movements coming toward the city, and he saw a man running toward the city.

18.22.0.en: The watchman called to the gatekeeper to tell the king about this man running toward the city, and the king was reassured, because it was customary that a messenger who came alone would usually bring joyful news, but if the news was not pleasant, more than one person would come in great sorrow.

18.23.0.en: After a short time the watchman saw another person also running alone toward the city (he was the Cushite), so the watchman called to the gatekeeper a second time to tell the king. And David said that he also was bringing good news since he was coming alone.

18.24.0.en: As the two men drew near one after the other, their features became clearer, and he knew that the first was Ahimaaz, and David remarked on this that Ahimaaz was a man of good tidings.

18.25.0.en: No sooner did Ahimaaz draw near the gate of the city than he called out to reassure the king, saying:

18.25.1.en: Peace, that is, all is well. And when he reached the king he bowed down before him and blessed the Lord, David's God, who had delivered into his hand the rebels who had resisted him.

18.26.0.en: David's concern was directed toward the safety of his son, so he hastened to ask Ahimaaz, "Is Absalom safe?" Ahimaaz was wise, for although he knew what had befallen Absalom, he did not wish to tell the king, but claimed that when Joab sent him and the Cushite to go to him, he saw a great crowd of people and did not know the reason for their gathering.

18.27.0.en: The king commanded him to stand where he was until the other messenger arrived, so that they might hear the news he brought.

18.28.0.en: Ahimaaz had hardly finished his report when the Cushite arrived where the king was and cried out with good news: Good tidings, my lord the king, for the Lord hath avenged thee this day of all them that rose up against thee.

18.29.0.en: The king was anxious for his son, so he hastened to ask the Cushite about his safety. The Cushite answered, praying that God would put to death all the enemies of the king as that young man had been put to death, and that their fate would be like his.

18.30.0.en: It was clear from the Cushite's words that Absalom had been killed in the battle, and the king was shaken by the news and went up to the chamber over the gate, and from the intensity of the inner turmoil that seized him he began to walk about in the chamber in deep sorrow, crying out, "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!", wishing that he had died instead of his son.

18.30.1.en: David's heart was full of fatherhood and mercy even toward his son who tried to kill him, and he wept bitterly over him at his death. May you be merciful and seek the salvation of sinners, even if they are your enemies and wrong you. David's return to the kingdom

19.0.s.en: (1) Joab rebukes David for his grief

19.0.0.en: Joab came back in great joy at having killed Absalom and triumphed over his armies, in preparation for David's return to his throne, and he expected to hear praise from David, or at least thanks to the commanders of his army and his soldiers for their great effort, but he was surprised to find David absorbed in his grief over Absalom's death, which of course affected the whole army, so that they were in gloom instead of joy.

19.1.0.en: The people too longed to hold victory celebrations for the great victory that had been achieved, but when they saw David weeping, grieving over the loss of his son, the celebrations turned to sorrow and the songs of victory were changed into a great mourning.

19.2.0.en: Instead of the soldiers entering the city of Mahanaim, where David was, exulting in the victory they had achieved, they entered the city in complete silence, with heads bowed, as if they were defeated soldiers.

19.3.0.en: David remained withdrawn into himself, covering his face with his hands from those around him, as though he did not wish to see anyone, repeating one cry in a loud voice: "O my son Absalom... O Absalom, my son... my son!"

19.4.0.en: Joab was not pleased with the king's attitude toward the victory that had been achieved, so he entered the house where the king was and rebuked him severely for his behavior toward his people and his disregard of them and of the effort they had made to achieve the victory, for they had saved his life and the lives of his sons, his wives and his concubines from being killed by Absalom had victory in the war been his.

19.5.0.en: Joab continued to reproach David, saying: You have shamed this day the faces of all your servants by your excessive grief over Absalom, who hated you and rebelled against you, while you did not appreciate what your men did, who loved you and fought for you. You have treated your men lightly as though they were of no account; indeed, perhaps you would be content with the death of all your soldiers and rejoice in the life of Absalom your enemy.

19.6.0.en: Joab urged David to stop his lamenting and go out to receive his soldiers who had come to congratulate him and to show them the appreciation due to them, and he warned him in a severe and harsh tone that if he did not, he would command his soldiers not to guard him, and he would spend the night alone in the tent and be exposed to being killed treacherously by anyone.

19.7.0.en: The king realized the seriousness of the matter, so he responded to Joab's warning, took courage, went out to the gate of the city and sat down. The warriors learned of the king's coming out, so they came to congratulate him on the victory, while Absalom's supporters were overtaken by shame and fled to their homes.

19.7.1.en: Do not indulge in your grief over the loss of one of your loved ones to the point of harming those around you, but be moderate, have hope in God, and ask for His help and consolation.

19.8.s.en: (2) All the tribes ask for David's return

19.8.0.en: After Absalom's death, the people were at odds with themselves, and each party began to blame the other for supporting Absalom, but they all agreed that David was the one who had saved them in the past from their enemies and from the Philistines, and that he had now left his throne in flight from Absalom, so he was the true king of the people.

19.9.0.en: Absalom, whom they had supported and anointed king over them, had been killed, and so the throne was empty of both David and Absalom, so the situation was not sound and matters had to be put right by their inviting David to reign over them and return to his throne.

19.10.0.en: David did not wish to return to his throne except on the basis of a new pledge of allegiance from the people. He had learned that the tribes of Israel, except the tribe of Judah, had all agreed on proclaiming him king again, so he sent Zadok and Abiathar, the two great priests, to Judah, reproaching them for their delay in inviting him to return to his throne in Jerusalem while the other tribes had preceded them in that invitation.

19.11.0.en: Among the things David said to the tribe of Judah was that they were his brethren, his bone and his flesh, because he himself was of the tribe of Judah, so it was not fitting for them to be behind the rest of the tribes in inviting him to return.

19.12.0.en: David wished to win to his side Amasa, who had been the commander of Absalom's army and was, besides, a skilled commander, so he asked the two priests to inform him that David reminded him of his kinship to him (for David was his maternal uncle), and that he had sworn to appoint him commander of his army for life in place of Joab (David was angry with Joab despite his loyalty and zeal for him, for he had done some things that angered David, such as his killing of Abner (ch. 3), his killing of Absalom (ch. 18), and the harshness of his rebuke of him when he was weeping for Absalom (vv. 5-7). By this action he won Amasa and all his soldiers who followed him, as they felt that David was the king who embraced all his people and forgave them their faults.

19.12.1.en: David here is a type of Christ, who transforms those subject to Satan "that is, Amasa, subject to Absalom"

19.12.2.en: into righteous people, servants in the Church of God, as He transformed Saul of Tarsus into the great Apostle Paul.

19.13.0.en: The men of the tribe of Judah responded to David's message, for they saw that although they had been behind the rest of the tribes in inviting him, he was not angry with them but spoke to them gently, so they came to themselves and remembered that they were indeed his kinsmen and that he belonged to their tribe, and they agreed to send to him inviting him to return to Jerusalem with all his men.

19.13.1.en: By wisdom, humility and gentle words David was able to put an end to the evil into which the tribe of Judah had fallen, for they were liable to split away from David under the leadership of Amasa, but by kindness he was able to win them, so they submitted to him and he won Amasa also. May you, by humility and kindness, face the angry and so break every evil that meets you, win those around you, and live in peace.

19.14.0.en: The king made ready on the bank east of the Jordan to cross, returning to Jerusalem, and at the same time the leading men of Judah reached Gilgal west of the Jordan on their way to cross to the east bank to receive the king there and bring him back to Jerusalem, the capital of the kingdom, which lies in the territory of their tribe.

19.15.0.en: Many came to meet David and welcome him on his way back to his throne in Jerusalem, and with them Shimei son of Gera, from the town of Bahurim, who had cursed the king and thrown stones and dust at him when he was fleeing from Absalom, trying by this to apologize for his fault, hoping that King David would be pleased with him (ch. 16:5).

19.16.0.en: Shimei came to receive the king with a delegation of a thousand men; so also came Ziba, who had been a servant of Saul and of his son Mephibosheth after him, accompanied by his fifteen sons and his twenty servants, and they crossed the Jordan River at the head of the returning king's procession.

19.16.1.en: Ziba came because he knew that the king would discover his deceit and his accusation against Mephibosheth, and so he wanted to appease the king.

19.17.0.en: Shimei prepared a special boat for the king and his household to cross in, putting himself at his service and ready to carry out his requests, and when Shimei met the king face to face he bowed down to the ground, showing respect and reverence for his person.

19.18.0.en: Shimei begged the king to forgive him what he had previously done against him of cursing and insult when he was fleeing from Absalom, and asked him not to keep any grudge against him in his heart.

19.19.0.en: The house of Joseph: he means that he came as the first group of the sons of Rachel, namely the tribes of Ephraim and Manasseh, the sons of Joseph, and the tribe of Benjamin, for Shimei wished to show how great his concern was, so he came as the first group of these three tribes.

19.19.1.en: Shimei confessed that he had indeed sinned when he had previously wronged the king, and here he was atoning for his fault by coming with his men to receive the king, so he was the first of the house of Joseph to come.

19.19.2.en: May we look at matters more deeply, so that we do not slip into actions we will regret later and whose remedy may become difficult, if not impossible, for we will not always meet a good-hearted person who forgives the one who wronged him, as David did.

19.20.0.en: Abishai son of Zeruiah was always impetuous in his zeal for David and loyalty to him, so he considered that everyone who was an enemy of David must be killed; in the past he asked David to kill Saul, and when Shimei was cursing David he asked his permission to kill him, and he now repeats his request because he saw that he had insulted David, the Lord's anointed. In addition, he felt that Shimei's apology was out of fear and not out of love, and perhaps it carried hypocrisy.

19.21.0.en: David rejected Abishai's proposal, because it was not fitting that anyone of God's people be killed; today was a day of joy for all, and there should be no mourning in any house of Israel, and he rebuked Abishai for not taking into account this day of joy at David's return to his throne once more. In addition, if Shimei were killed, then everyone who had been his enemy and joined Absalom ought to be killed too, and in this way a civil war could break out through the killing of many.

19.22.0.en: The king reassured Shimei and swore to him that no one would harm him. This was forbearance on David's part, although he knew that Shimei was insincere and deserved punishment, but he postponed that to the days of Solomon his son (1 Kgs 2:8, 9), and perhaps by this he gave Shimei an opportunity to repent and change his conduct, for his heart was not upright even now. David's forbearance toward Shimei was a waiver of his personal right against him, but Shimei had sinned against the Lord's anointed, so he had to be punished if he did not repent. Solomon warned him not to leave Jerusalem, but he left, and Solomon killed him. This signifies the one who goes outside the Church and so becomes liable to perdition. David here is a type of Christ on earth, who is forbearing toward those who wrong Him, and Solomon is a type of Christ in His glory when He judges the whole world.

19.23.0.en: Mephibosheth son of Jonathan was also among those who came to receive David, and it appeared from his look that he was very sad over the tragedies to which the king had been exposed, for he had neglected to care for his weak feet by applying some medical treatments to them, and he had not trimmed his beard or taken care of his clothes. All these signs contradict the slander in which Ziba had claimed that he was gloating over the tragic events that had befallen the king (ch. 16:3).

19.24.0.en: When Mephibosheth came to Jerusalem and met the king, the king reproached him for not accompanying him among the people who went out with him from Jerusalem when the rebellion arose.

19.25.0.en: Mephibosheth answered him that he had indeed intended to go out with the king, and had asked his servant Ziba to prepare a donkey for him to ride, since he was lame and could not walk long distances, but his servant Ziba deceived him, for he did not prepare the donkey for him, and went to the king by himself without taking him along.

19.26.0.en: Ziba was not content with that, but slandered me with what would inflame the king against me. And I know, my lord the king, that you are as an angel of God, able to distinguish between what is true and what is a false claim, and your judgment will be sound, so do what seems good to you.

19.27.0.en: I know the measure of your justice and compassion, for when you took the kingdom you could have killed all those left alive of the house of Saul, as kings do with the offspring of the kings who preceded them, but you did not do so; instead you honored me and invited me to your table as one of the members of your family, so after all this that you have done for me of kindness and honor, it is not right for me to covet a kingdom or authority, for David's accusation of Mephibosheth meant that he had stayed in Jerusalem out of covetousness for the kingdom after him.

19.28.0.en: The king asked him to stop speaking about matters that concerned him, for he had learned the truth of things before and had already corrected the situation, commanding that Mephibosheth take half the land and Ziba take the other half, because David had given all the possessions to Ziba and now corrected the situation by returning them to Mephibosheth, while Ziba would take half the produce in return for cultivating and looking after Mephibosheth's possessions. David was not harsh in punishing Ziba for his lie to David about Mephibosheth, because Ziba had done a good thing, namely not following Absalom but supporting David with food.

19.29.0.en: Mephibosheth showed no eagerness to recover the land, for he made clear to David that it did not matter to him much even if all of it went to Ziba, since his true joy was in the king's return to his seat in peace.

19.30.0.en: Rogelim: a city in the land of Gilead in which Barzillai lived. Its site today is "Wadi er-Rujayla" near Irbid.

19.30.1.en: Barzillai was one of the important figures who hosted David during his flight from Absalom, and he came to bid him farewell at the Jordan River on his return to his throne.

19.31.0.en: Crossing the Jordan was hard work for Barzillai, who had reached the age of eighty, but he bore it in honor of David, and he had already shown great love for the king, for when David was at Mahanaim he brought gifts and food for him and his companions and provided for them during their stay.

19.32.0.en: While they were crossing the Jordan, the king offered him to go with him to Jerusalem to live beside him, so that he might repay his kindness and honor him as Barzillai had honored him when he was at Mahanaim.

19.33.0.en: Barzillai excused himself because he was an old man of eighty and no longer could taste kinds of food or drink, nor enjoy the voices of the singing men and singing women who sing in the houses of kings. And he did not wish to be a burden to the king, for he needed special care of the kind the aged generally require, such as attention to certain kinds of food and a regular manner of life because of the weakness and sickness that are marks of old age.

19.34.0.en: He asked the king to bid him farewell by crossing the Jordan with him, even for a short distance, and then there would be no need of any other reward for him, for this honor was enough for him.

19.35.0.en: He asked permission to return afterward to his city, and when the time came to depart from this world, to be buried in the tomb of his father and mother, and if there had to be a reward, let his son Chimham cross over with the king, who would take him with him and honor him as he pleased in his place.

19.36.0.en: The king welcomed Barzillai's proposal to take Chimham with him, and promised to reward him as much as Barzillai wished for him, and to do for him and for Barzillai himself all that he asked. It is said that he became ruler of Bethlehem (Jer 41:17), and Jewish tradition says that in his house Christ was born when He became incarnate.

19.37.0.en: The king bade Barzillai farewell, kissing him with the kiss of love and asking the Lord's blessing for him, and he went back to his city in Gilead, and the people completed the crossing of the Jordan with the king.

19.37.1.en: Barzillai was an example to be followed in dignity and wisdom, and not like some of the aged who behave with a recklessness like the conduct of young boys. So let those of us who are advanced in years crown their old age with goodness and let their conduct be marked by balance and reason, so that they detach themselves from material things and prepare, by a spiritual life, for eternity.

19.38.0.en: The king crossed the Jordan River from east to west and reached the city of "Gilgal" near Jericho, and Chimham was in the king's company, as were also in his company the men of the tribe of Judah and half the tribes of Israel (the other half were late in coming at the proper time, perhaps because of the distance between the dwelling place of those tribes, which lived in the north of Palestine, and the region of "Gilgal"). In this way David took along many kinds of his people, for he is a type of Christ, who receives everyone:

19.38.1.en: 1 -The tribe of Judah: which signifies the whole Church.

19.38.2.en: 2 -Amasa: who signifies the wicked and rebellious whom God changes by repentance, so that they return to Him.

19.38.3.en: 3 -Shimei and Ziba: who signify sinners who try to repent.

19.38.4.en: 4 -Mephibosheth: who signifies broken and wronged souls.

19.38.5.en: 5 -Barzillai: who signifies the pious who are occupied with eternity.

19.38.6.en: 6 -Chimham: who signifies souls new to the faith.

19.39.0.en: Why have our brethren stolen thee away: the men of Judah monopolized the king in their celebration of his return.

19.39.1.en: When the rest of the tribes arrived after the king had crossed westward, they protested against the tribe of Judah, which, as they said, had monopolized the honoring of the king, and had crossed the Jordan with the king and his household without waiting for them to share in the honoring.

19.40.0.en: The tribe of Judah grew heated in answering the tribes' objection, claiming that the king was of their tribe and there was a bond of kinship between him and them, and that the tribes had no right to be angry at Judah's crossing with the king, and they said, Have we eaten at all of the king's cost? or hath he given us any gift? That is, we did not monopolize gifts we received from the king and did not obtain a special grant of which you were deprived.

19.41.0.en: The men of the tribes did not keep silent, but answered the men of Judah that they were the majority, for they represented ten tribes and Judah was one tribe, and therefore they had the greater right to bring the king back, and the men of Judah answered the men of the tribes with harsh words; that is, a quarrel of words took place between them.

19.41.1.en: The rebellion of Sheba son of Bichri
